QF.id: AIFM CII Fund Performance and Benchmarking_25

question.text: In the Alpha Fund worked-out case (Annexure 7.1 style): INR 700 cr drawn at Y0, INR 1300 cr at Y1; management fee + expenses INR 30 cr per year (Y0 onwards); first distribution not until Y4. Through which year would the J-curve typically show the deepest negative Gross FIRR?

answer.text: Y0 — because the first drawdown is the single largest cash outflow.
Y3 — end of the 2-year investment period plus one maturation year, just before first exits and while fees have accumulated for 4 years.
Y8 — because final winding-up catches all residual drag.

explanation.text: **The Logic:** The J-curve trough is the point of MAXIMUM NEGATIVE cumulative cash flow before exits begin. Drawdowns are complete by Y1 (INR 2000 cr deployed) and fees/expenses continue piling up (30 x 4 = INR 120 cr by Y3) with zero realisations till Y3. Once Y4 distributions begin, cumulative cash flow starts climbing. The trough is at Y3. **The Trap:** Y0 is the single largest year outflow but not the deepest cumulative point (more fees to come). Y5 is after 2 distribution years — recovering. Y8 is the peak (wind-up), not trough. **Cross-Exam Context:** XIX-C uses the same J-curve mechanics. Global PE texts (Gottschalg, Kaplan) call Y3-Y4 the 'valley of death' for vintage returns. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** Chart the J-curve quarterly and include the 'cumulative paid-in capital' line in LP reports — LPs who see the trough explained in advance rarely panic when Y3 Net IRR shows -8%.
